65fc387dcb.q: What specific problem did Boyd's software address in field auditing and reporting?
65fc387dcb.a: Field auditors had to drive to job sites, spend two to three hours performing audits, drive back, and type up reports at night with pictures and notes,…
65fc387dcb.e: A personal touch: elevating safety compliance through technology and leadership
f: Field auditors once spent two to three hours on-site conducting audits, then drove back to the office to type reports at night with photographs and notes—creating a critical delay before leadership could act on safety issues. Boyd's software solved this by enabling real-time photo uploads and instant report distribution, eliminating the gap and freeing auditors from desk work after hours.

Before the software existed, the workflow was linear and slow. An auditor would drive to a job site, spend the afternoon performing a full compliance audit, drive back—sometimes hours away—and then spend their evening documenting findings with pictures and handwritten notes, creating a multi-day lag before any corrective action could begin . This delay meant safety issues lingered unaddressed, and employees burned out from after-hours administrative burden.

The core insight came from Boyd's own management of safety compliance across 1,200 employees across approximately 24 different U.S. locations at an oilfield services company starting in 2011. He experienced firsthand how even critical safety findings—like a five-week delay on a rattlesnake safety observation card—could get lost in manual reporting systems. That frustration led him to co-found a safety software company in 2014 with two partners to solve exactly this problem.
"When technology gets used for people to be people, to give humans more time to do other things, that's where the positive impact from a safety perspective happens."

Darren Boyd — SVP of new markets at KPA services. Boyd began his career in collegiate athletics as director of basketball operations at the University of Oklahoma before moving into operations and health and safety leadership in the oilfield services sector. His experience managing compliance at scale led him to recognize the gap between field reality and office reporting, motivating him to build technology that kept people connected to relationships rather than chained to screens after work hours.

The software Boyd's company developed—which was later acquired by KPA services—changed the game by automating the middle steps. Field auditors could now upload photos directly from the job site in real time, and reports flowed instantly to leadership decision-makers. This eliminated the overnight typing bottleneck and accelerated response to safety findings by days or even weeks . As a bonus, it restored work-life balance by keeping auditors off desks after hours, a human benefit that matters as much as the operational speed gain.

f8f6daa125.q: How does Darren Boyd believe technology should be used in safety management?
f8f6daa125.a: Boyd believes that when technology is used to give humans more time to do other things, that is where positive safety impact happens. Technology should push…
f8f6daa125.e: A personal touch: elevating safety compliance through technology and leadership
f: Technology works best in safety management when it gives professionals more time away from their desks to spend in the field , not when it automates or replaces human interaction. Building trust and relationships with employees cannot happen through screens—it happens standing beside them, performing tasks together.
Technology as a Tool for Field Engagement

The core of Boyd's philosophy is straightforward: technology should liberate safety professionals, not confine them. When a software system handles administrative burdens—reporting, data entry, compliance tracking—it creates the opportunity for safety teams to do what matters most: build genuine relationships with the workforce.

This principle emerged from Boyd's own experience. After taking over the health and safety department at an oilfield services company managing 1,200 employees across 24 U.S. locations , he discovered that the existing workflow was deeply broken. Pre-software, he would spend hours each week driving to job sites, conducting audits, and then typing up reports at night. The administrative overhead was so heavy that meaningful field presence became impossible. When Boyd later co-founded his safety software company in 2014, this pain point became the design priority, as detailed in the Inspiring Industry Podcast episode .
Why Automation Cannot Replace Trust-Building

Some companies are experimenting with automating safety meetings entirely—letting AI guide pre-job briefings or compliance checks. Boyd sees this as a critical mistake. Automating a meeting doesn't accomplish what a meeting is meant to do.

Getting one rep in, every single day

The sports analogy Boyd relies on most is remarkably simple. Just like an athlete builds muscle through consistent daily practice , a safety culture strengthens when teams commit to small, repeated actions. Being better than yesterday is the metric—not a dramatic leap forward, but genuine progress through compounded effort.

This philosophy extends directly to how Boyd views the relationship between a safety organization and the people it serves. When technology gets used to create space for humans to work together on shared tasks—rather than replacing human judgment—that's where real safety gains emerge. As Boyd explains in the episode , trust and relationships are built standing next to somebody performing a task together , never behind a computer screen.
The coaching mindset applied to safety adoption

Boyd developed a presentation built directly on Ted Lasso's leadership philosophy—the TV character known for unconditional belief in team potential. He connects coaching principles directly to how organizations adopt new safety processes and technology . A coach doesn't demand excellence; a coach creates conditions where people want to give their best effort, because they know their teammates will do the same.

8cfc98263a.q: How did SPEE3D develop its metal 3D printing technology and what problem was it designed to solve?
8cfc98263a.a: Byron Kennedy and his partner Steve Committery developed SPEE3D around 2015-2016 after discovering a technology used by the US military for repair that was very manual. They thought they could take this manual spray process, add sophistication and software, and build a technology that was fast and low cost—addressing the reality that traditional metal 3D printing was too expensive and too slow for production environments.
8cfc98263a.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: Byron Kennedy and Steve Committery discovered a manual spray process used by the US military for repairs around 2015–2016, then automated and enhanced it with software to create SPEE3D. The result was a metal 3D printing technology 100 to 1,000 times faster and dramatically more affordable than traditional metal additive manufacturing —solving the industry's critical problem that production-level metal 3D printing was too slow and expensive to be economically viable.
From military repair process to scalable manufacturing technology

Kennedy and Committery recognized that the manual military spray technique contained genuine potential, but it lacked the sophistication needed for real production environments. They understood that traditional metal 3D printing solutions were fundamentally uneconomical: the technology worked in principle, but the speed and cost barriers made it impractical for manufacturing at scale .

The pair took the core military process and engineered it into an automated system with embedded software intelligence. This wasn't simply a matter of making the existing technique faster—it was about rethinking the entire value proposition. As Kennedy explains in the podcast , the transformation enabled manufacturers to eliminate moulds entirely and bypass the need for massive, capital-intensive factories.
Why speed and cost matter in real manufacturing

In manufacturing, downtime doesn't just mean delay—it means catastrophic financial loss . Consider a mining operation: if a critical part fails and cannot be replaced immediately, the cost can reach $1 million per day. SPEE3D's approach directly addresses this nightmare scenario. By enabling on-site production of replacement parts in hours rather than weeks, the technology transforms manufacturing resilience.

11e0735a11.q: What are the speed advantages of SPEE3D's technology compared to other metal 3D printing technologies?
11e0735a11.a: SPEE3D is typically between 100 to 1,000 times faster than other metal 3D printing technologies. At those speeds, the technology can compete with traditional casting, which has been around for 5,000 years. This speed advantage enables manufacturers to eliminate the need for moulds and large capital-intensive factories, allowing them to build one part, ten parts, or 10,000 parts with the same equipment.
11e0735a11.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective

80706b7637.q: How has SPEE3D deployed its technology with defense forces globally?
80706b7637.a: Starting around 2019, the Australian Army approached SPEE3D to deploy the four-ton printer in the field. After testing and refinements during COVID, SPEE3D is now working with five defense forces across the globe, with 10 systems deployed to Ukraine. The company also became the first to manufacture metal parts on a US naval ship and has completed testing at sub-freezing conditions with defense forces.
80706b7637.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: SPEE3D began deploying its four-ton metal 3D printer with the Australian Army around 2019, and today operates across five defense forces globally with 10 systems in Ukraine . The company has become the first to manufacture metal parts aboard a US Navy ship and completed cold-weather testing with military partners.
From pilot program to global defense deployment

The journey started when the Australian Army approached SPEE3D in 2019 with a clear operational need: field-deployable metal manufacturing. After iterative testing and refinements during the COVID period, the concept moved from proof-of-concept to active deployment. The systems proved their value on the ground, particularly in environments where traditional supply chains couldn't deliver critical spare parts quickly enough.

By 2024, SPEE3D had grown its defense footprint to working partnerships with five military forces across multiple continents. The Ukraine deployment alone represents the largest concentration of SPEE3D systems in active use, with 10 units in the field supporting military operations and maintenance needs. As discussed in this episode of Inspiring Industry Podcast , the speed advantage of the technology—being 100 to 1,000 times faster than conventional metal 3D printing—directly translates to operational readiness in conflict zones.
First metal parts manufactured at sea

One of SPEE3D's most significant milestones came when it became the first company to manufacture metal components aboard a US Navy vessel . This breakthrough demonstrated that the technology could operate reliably in one of the harshest and most demanding environments imaginable—shipboard operations with strict power, space, and quality constraints. The achievement validated the robustness of the platform beyond land-based defense applications.

234d5a14e1.q: What is SPEE3D's unique market positioning within the broader 3D printing industry?
234d5a14e1.a: Unlike the metal 3D printing industry which focused on slow, very precise or very complex parts, SPEE3D targeted commodity, low-cost, fast parts—a completely different market segment. Kennedy emphasizes that 3D printing is a tool like any other with advantages and disadvantages, and each technology has its sweet spot. SPEE3D chose to push cost down and speed up rather than pursue absolute perfection, deliberately taking the industry into a different area.
234d5a14e1.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: SPEE3D deliberately rejected the metal 3D printing industry's obsession with precision and complexity to target an entirely different market: fast, low-cost commodity parts that traditional manufacturing couldn't serve efficiently. Rather than pursuing absolute perfection, the company chose to push speed and affordability—a strategic pivot that created a completely new market segment in additive manufacturing.
Speed and cost over precision: a different game

The conventional metal 3D printing industry had spent years optimizing for slow, extremely precise, or highly complex parts—the assumption being that additive manufacturing's value lay in geometric perfection. Kennedy and his team saw the problem differently. As explained in the episode , the team discovered technology originally developed by the US military that offered a radically different path: manufacturing parts 100 to 1,000 times faster than conventional metal 3D printing, at a fraction of the cost.

This wasn't about competing in the same market. SPEE3D deliberately chose to move the industry into an entirely different space. Kennedy emphasizes that 3D printing, like any manufacturing tool, has distinct advantages and disadvantages—and the key is understanding which technology solves which problem best. For SPEE3D, that meant targeting applications where speed and economics mattered far more than micron-level precision.
The manufacturing constraint problem: where speed becomes profit

The real-world problem SPEE3D solves is tangible and costly. Consider a mining operation where a critical part fails and cannot be sourced locally: downtime can cost $1 million per day . In such scenarios, the ability to manufacture a replacement part on-site in hours—rather than waiting weeks for traditional manufacturing or paying for emergency logistics—fundamentally changes the economics of operations.

2123751017.q: How does leadership philosophy influence talent attraction and team motivation at SPEE3D?
2123751017.a: Kennedy and Steve follow the leadership philosophies from Jim Collins' book 'Good to Great,' emphasizing mathematical rigor and evidence-based decision-making. They attract top talent by tackling challenging problems using high-speed robotics, rocket nozzles, and sophisticated software algorithms in emerging sectors like defense and space. They keep teams motivated through iterative problem-solving based on engineering principles: forming a hypothesis, testing it, and iterating when it doesn't work, while being willing to pull the pin on ideas that don't succeed.
2123751017.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: SPEE3D's founders embrace evidence-based decision-making principles from Jim Collins' "Good to Great," using mathematical rigor to guide leadership choices. They attract top talent by tackling genuinely difficult engineering problems in emerging sectors like defense and space using high-speed robotics and sophisticated software. Teams stay motivated through a disciplined iterative cycle—form a hypothesis, test it rigorously, learn from failure, and move on when ideas don't work.
Leadership anchored in evidence, not intuition

Byron Kennedy and Steve Committery built SPEE3D's leadership culture on a foundational principle: decisions must be grounded in data and scientific method, not guesswork. This philosophy, drawn directly from Jim Collins' strategic work, shapes how they hire, how they set direction, and how they evaluate whether an approach is actually working.

The discipline shows up in daily practice. Rather than pushing forward with a solution because it feels promising, Kennedy and Committery insist teams form explicit hypotheses, run controlled tests, and examine the results with ruthless honesty. When evidence points away from an idea, they're willing to abandon it—a clarity that removes the ego from failure and keeps the organization moving toward what actually works.
Attracting engineers through hard problems

Top talent gravitates toward teams solving problems that matter. SPEE3D draws world-class engineers by offering access to some of the most challenging technical puzzles in manufacturing—deploying high-speed robotics, designing rocket nozzles, and building sophisticated algorithms for emerging sectors like defense and aerospace.

88050f3159.q: What are the primary industrial sectors SPEE3D is targeting for growth beyond defense?
88050f3159.a: In 2024, SPEE3D is focusing on heavy industry sectors including mining, oil and gas, rail, marine, and automotive—industries facing severe supply chain problems. Kennedy notes that if a mine site cannot get a critical part, it might cost $1 million a day in downtime. Being able to build a part locally and immediately is highly attractive to these industries, which is why SPEE3D's ideal business mix is 50% defense and 50% heavy industry, with current operations at approximately 80% defense.
88050f3159.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: SPEE3D is pivoting toward five heavy industrial sectors—mining, oil and gas, rail, marine, and automotive—where supply chain failures carry catastrophic costs. The company's target is a 50–50 split between defense and heavy industry revenue , though current operations remain at approximately 80% defense.
The million-dollar downtime problem

These five sectors share a common pain point: dependency on spare parts for critical operations. When a mine site cannot source a replacement component, the financial impact is severe. As Kennedy explains in the episode , the cost of a single day's downtime on a mine site can reach $1 million daily —a loss that accrues hour by hour until the part is available.

SPEE3D's value proposition addresses this directly: local, immediate manufacturing of replacement parts eliminates the delay and expense of traditional supply chains. For industries operating at scale—mining operations, offshore drilling rigs, railway networks—the ability to manufacture a critical part onsite transforms downtime from a catastrophic event into a manageable interruption.
Why heavy industry is the natural next market

Heavy industry and defense face fundamentally similar manufacturing challenges: the need for rapid part production under extreme operational constraints. Defense deployments require field-level manufacturing capability; mining and oil extraction require the same resilience against supply disruption. Kennedy's strategy recognizes this overlap—both sectors value speed and local control over manufacturing destiny.

e38f26058a.q: Why should manufacturers evaluate and adopt new 3D printing technologies rather than rely solely on traditional casting?
e38f26058a.a: The manufacturing sector is moving and evolving in a positive direction, driven by digital technologies and new innovations. Kennedy advises that manufacturers must evaluate new technologies quickly to determine if they are right for their specific application, and if they don't adopt them, their competitors will. The key is to discount technologies rapidly and say yes or no, then move forward accordingly rather than getting caught up in hype.
e38f26058a.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: The manufacturing sector is moving forward through digital innovation and new technologies, but success requires manufacturers to evaluate new solutions quickly and make decisive commitments . If you hesitate while competitors adopt them, you risk losing competitive ground—not because the technology is guaranteed to work for everyone, but because speed and adaptability now define market leadership.

Casting has dominated manufacturing for 5,000 years, and that longevity creates natural reluctance to change. Yet the question manufacturers face today is not whether to abandon all traditional methods, but rather which parts and applications benefit most from a faster approach . As Byron Kennedy explains in the episode , the real cost of inaction shows up in critical downtime situations—on a mine site, a single unavailable part can cost a million dollars per day.
Why speed matters more than you think

Traditional manufacturing requires expensive infrastructure: moulds, large factories, and capital-intensive equipment. 3D printing removes that barrier . When you eliminate the need for a mould, you no longer need that massive facility or that heavy upfront investment to manufacture parts. Instead, you can build them on-demand and on-location when the need arises .

This shift is especially powerful in remote operations—mining sites, offshore rigs, military field deployments—where supply chains are fragile and delays are expensive. A four-ton printer, roughly the size of a small car, can now sit on location and produce critical components in hours instead of weeks.
The competitive window is narrow

cc553785cf.q: What distinguishes SPEE3D's approach to R&D and product commercialization from perfectionist development?
cc553785cf.a: Kennedy explains that SPEE3D does not wait for perfect products before commercializing. The company releases an 80% product to get market feedback before taking the next steps. This pragmatic approach reflects their philosophy that sometimes what you have is good enough and you need to stop perfecting and start commercializing to understand real customer needs.
cc553785cf.e: Challenges and innovations in 3D printing: SPEE3D's perspective
f: SPEE3D releases products at 80% completion to capture real market feedback and understand genuine customer needs, rather than pursuing endless perfectionism. This pragmatic philosophy recognizes that sometimes what you have is good enough—and the only way to truly improve is to commercialize, learn from the field, and iterate based on actual usage.
Perfectionism kills commercialization

The core distinction between SPEE3D's approach and traditional product development is a fundamental shift in mindset. Byron Kennedy explains that in the episode , the company does not spend years refining a product in the lab before it touches a customer. Instead, 80% is the threshold for entry into the market —good enough to work, incomplete enough to teach you what matters.

This decision reflects a deeper truth about manufacturing innovation: the gap between what engineers think customers need and what they actually need is often only revealed in the field. Waiting for 100% perfection before commercialization delays that learning and leaves you exposed to competitors who move faster.
Market feedback beats theory

By releasing an 80% product, SPEE3D gains access to something no lab can provide: real-world operational data and genuine customer pain points . A mining operation running one of their metal 3D printers on-site will surface problems and opportunities that internal testing never would. Field deployment teaches you which features matter, which don't, and where the next breakthrough lies.

3e9bd73a72.q: What are the main misconceptions about renewable fuels and the energy transition that Topsoe addresses?
3e9bd73a72.a: The biggest misconception is that renewable fuels will be the same cost as fossil fuels, which they are not. Another major misconception is that we're about to phase out oil and gas entirely. Without government mandates and incentives, renewable fuel projects simply will not happen because they are significantly more expensive than fossil alternatives.
3e9bd73a72.e: Topsoe's roadmap to renewables: How multiple pathways will drive the energy transition.

3d90679f38.q: How is the Inflation Reduction Act signed into law in 2022 impacting Topsoe and the broader energy sector?
3d90679f38.a: The IRA is a game changer for Topsoe because the company's basket of technologies in decarbonization is perfectly aligned with the legislation. Topsoe has licensed the vast majority of projects in renewable jet, diesel, blue ammonia, and blue hydrogen. The IRA has fueled economic growth by generating these projects and creating employment throughout the US economy.
3d90679f38.e: Topsoe's roadmap to renewables: How multiple pathways will drive the energy transition.
f: The IRA is a game changer for Topsoe because the company's basket of technologies in decarbonization aligns perfectly with the legislation. Topsoe has licensed the vast majority of projects in renewable jet, diesel, blue ammonia, and blue hydrogen , and the act has fueled economic growth by generating these projects and creating employment throughout the US economy.
A perfectly aligned regulatory framework

When the Inflation Reduction Act passed in 2022, Topsoe found itself in an exceptional position. The company's portfolio of clean energy technologies—spanning sustainable aviation fuel, renewable diesel, blue ammonia, and blue hydrogen—matched almost exactly what the legislation incentivized.

As Henrik Rasmussen explains in the episode , this alignment was not accidental. Topsoe had spent years developing technologies to address the decarbonization challenge—the IRA simply created the economic incentives that turned those technologies into viable commercial projects.

The legislation accelerated project deployment significantly . By providing tax credits and investment subsidies for renewable fuels and hydrogen production, the act removed many of the financial barriers that had previously slowed commercialization. Projects that had been stuck in planning phases suddenly became economically feasible.
From licensing leadership to employment growth

bf56180bb2.q: What multiple pathways does Topsoe pursue for the energy transition instead of relying on a single solution?
bf56180bb2.a: Topsoe pursues several pathways including sustainable aviation fuel from fats, oils and greases; blue ammonia and blue hydrogen using natural gas with CO2 sequestration; green fuels and green ammonia from renewable electricity; and continued investment in more efficient fossil fuel catalysts. Each pathway comes at different times due to different stages of commercialization and scale, and all are needed because there is no single silver bullet solution.
bf56180bb2.e: Topsoe's roadmap to renewables: How multiple pathways will drive the energy transition.

ba1b7ec6e6.q: Why does Topsoe believe nuclear energy will play a role in the energy transition going forward?
ba1b7ec6e6.a: Nuclear is ultimately decarbonized electricity at scale and can fuel the green wave at a higher scale than wind and solar alone. There is only limited room on the globe for solar panels and windmills while still needing land to grow crops, so nuclear must be part of the combination of energy sources required for the transition.
ba1b7ec6e6.e: Topsoe's roadmap to renewables: How multiple pathways will drive the energy transition.

a09825d936.q: What does Topsoe identify as the key barrier to financing sustainable aviation fuel projects despite having proven technology?
a09825d936.a: Even when airlines sign long-term offtake agreements for sustainable aviation fuel, financing communities are reluctant to invest because they view airlines as non-investment grade companies that may not survive 20 years. The airlines, consumers, financing community, and governments must all align on mandates, incentives, and willingness to pay premium prices for SAF to make projects viable and reach financial close.
a09825d936.e: Topsoe's roadmap to renewables: How multiple pathways will drive the energy transition.

0ee70f1271.a: Topsoe was founded in 1940 with the principle that the business world itself does not make sense unless it does something to better mankind. The company's motto is to perfect chemistry for a better world. Starting with addressing starvation through ammonia fertilizer plants in the 1950s in Bangladesh and India, the company has evolved to tackle successive global challenges including air pollution, acid rain, and now decarbonization.
